text: There are subjects you steer around, and the steering shows. The old astrologers kept the Lot of Nemesis for whatever a person declines to face, and yours stands in the first house, the house that enters the room before anything else about you does. So your avoidances are worn, not stored. The flinch at a certain name, the joke deployed half a second too fast, the topic that makes you reach for your glass: what you have put away does not sit in some remote corner of your life. It rides along in person, and people who pay attention can trace its outline long before you describe it, because the outline is part of how you carry yourself. Nothing postponed stays anonymous for you. When a buried thing finally comes up, it comes up to your face, in a room you are standing in, usually while you are mid-sentence. You do not get to read about your reckonings later; you attend them. Speed is the compensation, and it is a large one. Self-deception needs distance to grow in, and you have none to offer it. An avoidance in you starts prickling almost immediately, itching like a label in a collar, and that early discomfort is the cheapest warning system a person can own. Most people learn what they were refusing to look at years afterward, from wreckage. You get told in real time, by your own restlessness, while the thing is still small enough to face between breakfast and lunch. The practice that fits this arrangement is modest. When you catch yourself steering, look once, briefly, at what you steered around: not a full excavation, just a glance, enough to keep the thing named and current. Named things stay portable. It is the unnamed ones that grow heavy, and your chart, mercifully, has made you bad at leaving things unnamed. The result, after enough repetitions, is a hard-won lightness. You carry less than most people, not because less has happened to you, but because so little of what happened was ever allowed to go underground.

Somewhere in what you own there is a decision you have not made. The second house covers property and livelihood, and the Lot of Nemesis stationed there means your postponements take physical form. The subscription that keeps renewing because canceling it would mean looking at it. The inherited object kept out of guilt rather than love. The drawer of things that are really unfinished questions: return it, repair it, admit it was a mistake. Avoidance, in your life, takes up shelf space. Money behaves the same way. Whatever you would rather not know about your material situation does not vanish for being unexamined; it goes vague, and vagueness has a direction. The unopened envelope, the number known only approximately, the conversation about what things cost that keeps being scheduled for tomorrow: each stays quiet a long while and then stops being quiet all at once, usually through some small event that drags the whole subject into daylight in a single afternoon. None of this is a curse on your resources. It is a plain mechanism, and it runs in reverse just as reliably. Material facts faced while they are ordinary stay ordinary. The same envelope, opened monthly, never becomes a monster, and the same drawer, sorted one object at a time, quietly gives back its shelf. People who live with this point in this house often discover that the dread was the heaviest part of the whole business, and that the facts underneath were almost disappointingly manageable. What grows here, slowly, is a taste for plain sight. You come to want to know what you hold, what it needs from you, and what it is standing in for, because a thing you can see clearly can no longer gain weight in the dark.

The third house is short roads and familiar faces: siblings, neighbors, the weekly call, the errands that repeat. Your Lot of Nemesis keeps its station there, so the things you would rather not face are never far away, and they have your schedule. The subject you and a sibling have not touched in years attends every visit anyway. The situation next door that everyone manages around sits inside each over-the-fence hello. The message read and never answered waits at the bottom of a thread you use daily. At close range, an avoidance is never truly out of sight; it comes to the barbecue, and it lives in the pause before certain names. When it finally comes up, it tends to come up casually, mid-errand, in a doorway, at the least ceremonial venue available, because near things return through near channels. The withheld word deserves watching here too: the correction you did not make, the plain answer softened into fog, the small no swallowed to keep Tuesday smooth. Each feels like courtesy on the day and reads differently in a year. What this position teaches, sometimes comically, is how differently the same conversation goes depending on when you have it. The dreaded five-minute talk, had early, takes five minutes. Postponed, it grows a season of rehearsals, detours, and managed encounters heavier than any argument would have been. You learn to spend the five minutes. And the near world, which was never the enemy, goes back to being what it is for everyone else: short roads, familiar faces, and nothing under the pavement with your name on it.

Whatever you managed not to feel today is waiting where you sleep. The fourth house sits at the bottom of the chart, and your Lot of Nemesis rests there, in the place a life goes when it stops performing: the household, the evening, the people who see you with your shoes off. Out in the world, putting a thing aside works, because there are meetings and errands and other people's noise to stand in front of it. At home the noise stops, and the put-aside thing comes quietly out of the walls. This is why your avoidances have a domestic signature. They rarely erupt at work; they thicken the air at dinner. A postponed grief shows up as a short temper about dishes. An unsaid sentence between two people becomes a heaviness in the room that guests can feel without being able to name. Households are honest instruments: they register what their members refuse to say, and the reading appears as atmosphere. Some of what lies under your floor was there before you arrived. Most families hand down a subject or two wrapped in silence, and one of yours may be doing its waiting in your house now, which is not a fault and not a sentence, only an address. What matters is the direction of travel while you are the resident. Buried things at home hold one great advantage over buried things anywhere else: home is also the safest place there is to let them up. Nobody has to manage an audience. The kitchen table at ten at night, one person, one true sentence: a reckoning of this kind is so much gentler than the public sort that it barely deserves the same word. A household where the hard thing can be said out loud, even badly, even in pieces, stops accumulating atmosphere, and the change is physical. The air moves. The rooms feel larger. People sleep. You have more say in this than anyone else under the roof, because the point is yours, and a custom is a thing one person can start. Say the true thing at the table often enough and the house learns it. What reached you underground can end above ground, in words, on your watch, and evenings in a house like that end lighter than the days that led to them.

The fifth house is where a chart keeps its delight: romance, play, children, the things people make because making them feels good. Yours also houses the Lot of Nemesis, and the pairing is stranger than it first sounds. A lot is a point computed from the chart rather than a planet standing in it, and this one belongs to Saturn, marking whatever gets put away instead of faced. What you put away, it turns out, is usually joy. The instrument in the closet. The manuscript that is safest unwritten, because unwritten it can still be brilliant. The invitation never issued, the game never joined, the wholehearted enthusiasm trimmed down to an ironic hobby you could disown if anyone laughed. What goes underground in your life is not your worst material but some of your best, buried to keep it from being judged. Buried delight does not keep quiet, though. It returns as restlessness in the middle of pleasant evenings, and as a strange sharpness toward people doing, clumsily and in public, the exact thing you have been keeping pristine and private. That sting rewards close reading; it is rarely about the other person. Romance lives in this house too, and the same reflex operates there: the light tone maintained to dodge a real conversation, the preference kept secret because stating it risks the mood. Affection managed that carefully goes thin, and part of you notices before the rest of you admits it. Confidence would fix all this, but confidence takes years, and smallness takes a week. The shelved thing let out at miniature scale: one page shown to one person, one song played badly on purpose, one honest preference stated on an ordinary night. Delight recovers fast once it gets daylight, faster than almost anything else a person can bury, and it holds no grudge about the years in storage. The pleasure was never lost. It was waiting for you to stop guarding it.

The task at the bottom of your list has been there for a year, and it is not dying. With the Lot of Nemesis in the sixth house, the house of daily work and daily upkeep, your schedule is more than a plan; it is a map of what you are not choosing. The conversation with a colleague that keeps losing to urgent trivia. The workload accepted again this month because renegotiating it would mean saying a true thing out loud. The one recurring errand that somehow never recurs. Avoidance here does not hide in dramatic places. It hides inside busyness, the best camouflage ever invented, since nobody interrogates a person who is visibly working. Your body tends to know about a postponement before you admit to one. The shoulders that climb toward your ears in certain meetings, the tiredness that follows one duty and not another, the appetite that goes strange during a particular stretch of the job: these signals arrive early and in small print, and they are not malfunctions. They are the most honest colleagues you have. The pattern breaks at the same scale it formed, which is daily. One avoided item moved to the top of one morning, once a week, changes the character of the entire list. The conversation had in week two instead of month eight turns out to be a workday event rather than a crisis. And this house repays plain dealing unusually fast. A routine with no refusals folded into it runs lighter than its length explains, and you can feel the difference on the first ordinary morning after the long-avoided thing is simply, finally, done.

The person across the table knows where your buried things are, and not because you told them. The seventh house belongs to the people you face directly, spouses, partners, close collaborators, declared rivals, and your Lot of Nemesis stands among them, which means what you decline to look at does not stay out of view; it gets represented. A partner keeps arriving at the one subject you route around, innocently, from a new angle each time. The recurring argument in a long relationship turns out, on inspection, to be the same argument wearing different clothes, returning at intervals like an appointment you keep rescheduling. Even your opponents participate. The criticism that stings for days is rarely the unfair one; it is the one with coordinates, the remark that lands precisely on the spot you have been keeping out of your own sight. People who face you seem to read your avoided places with unsettling accuracy, and there is a reason: at close range, over time, the avoided places are the most visible thing about anyone. Two cautions keep this from souring. The first is not to punish the couriers. A partner who names your buried thing is doing dangerous, valuable work, usually out of love, and if the naming costs them a week of frost, the naming stops. What follows is a polite relationship organized around a growing silence, the loneliest arrangement two people can share. The second caution is to remember that the traffic runs both ways. You carry a matching ability to see what the person opposite you is not facing, and the same rules apply to your mouth as to theirs: accuracy is not a license, timing is half of kindness, and some things are theirs to reach in their own year. Handled with those cautions, this position turns close relationships into something the solitary never get. Nothing stays buried long between you and the people who matter, which sounds exhausting and is actually the opposite. Couples and old friends who cannot hide from each other stop spending strength on hiding. The subjects come up while they are small. The recurring argument, once recognized as recurring, can finally be had properly, once, all the way through, after which it loses its appointment slot. And a quiet upgrade sits inside the whole design: the person who knew where your buried things were is also the person who knows, better than anyone, how far you have traveled from them. Being seen that completely, and staying, is about as close to safety as human beings arrange.

Some subjects wait for an ending to authorize them. A partnership closes, a will is read, a crisis burns off the small talk, and suddenly things are said that were sayable for years, to people who would have listened at any point. Your Lot of Nemesis in the eighth house makes you a student of exactly this delay. The eighth is where lives go deepest into each other, and what Nemesis marks there is the material two people put away together: the subject a couple retires by unspoken treaty, the question about the shared money or the shared future that stays unasked because asking feels like disloyalty, the grief a whole family agrees, without a meeting, to skip. Joint avoidance is sturdier than the private kind, because everyone involved is guarding the same door. It also breaks the same way for everyone at once. The event that marks this house for you is the ending that reveals: the parting that shows what the relationship was never saying, the loss that brings up an older loss that never got its season, the emergency in which two people finally have the conversation the calm years kept declining. You have likely stood in a few of these rooms already, and noticed something about yourself there. You can bear the moment when the real subject stands up better than most; where others edge toward the exits, something in you goes still and pays attention, almost relieved. That steadiness is the gift half of the arrangement, and it deserves conscious use. The practice this house rewards is borrowing the honesty of a crisis without waiting for one. The deep subjects, what you are to each other, what you both know and never say, which goodbye you are pretending is a postponement, can be opened on a calm evening by somebody brave, and you are positioned to be that somebody. Spoken in fair weather, these conversations turn out quiet, even tender, and they change what the hard weather can do when it comes. Not everything can be prepared for, and nothing here promises exemption from loss. What changes is the aftermath. The endings that arrive in a life like this find less unsaid material waiting for them, and the people who shared the depths with you get to grieve only the loss itself, not the years of silence around it.

The ninth house holds conviction, long study, and the wide view, and your Lot of Nemesis lives there, which means what you would rather not face tends to hide inside what you are sure of. The mechanism looks respectable. A hard personal question gets answered with a principle, and the principle is then defended so the question never has to be reopened. A worldview gets adopted whole, in a difficult season, because it organized the chaos, and years later it is still on duty, guarding a door you have forgotten is there. Certainty, in you, sometimes has the specific warmth of something working hard. The reckonings of this house arrive through its own channels. The book read past the chapter that agreed with you. The student, or the friend, whose plain question you cannot answer without noticing you never answered it for yourself. The country that declines to be the country you had described to everyone back home. Moments like these feel like attacks on your foundations, and they are actually deliveries: a buried question coming back up through the one channel you left open, your real interest in what is true. Nothing here says your convictions are wrong. It says some of them are load-bearing in a way that has nothing to do with their truth, and those are the ones worth finding, because a belief doing secret protective work cannot also do honest work. The test is mild and private. Which of your certainties are you unwilling to question, and what would be so bad about the answer? Beliefs that survive that question come back sturdier and lighter, held by choice instead of by need, and the question itself stops circling the house once it has been let in. The ones that do not survive were not holding up the roof. You find you can stand there anyway.

Nemesis carries the most ominous name in the lot tradition, and the name oversells it: the point hands down no verdicts, yours included. The lots are computed places rather than planets, each keeping one theme, and Saturn's keeps the theme nobody requests, the put-off, the postponed, the thing that returns to be dealt with. Standing in the tenth house, at the most public height of your chart, it adds a single condition to the returning: witnesses. What comes back for you tends to come back at work, in the professional record, in front of exactly the people you would have chosen last. The corner cut early in a project shows in the finished thing, at the demonstration. The overstated claim meets an audience containing the one person who knows. The unresolved private matter picks launch week. Colleagues with easier arrangements let things slide for years; your career seems fitted with a mechanism that routes the slid thing back on stage. Read as persecution, that curdles a person. Read as design, it is a strict teacher with one lesson: handle it while it is private. You get the same choice everyone gets, face the thing now or face it later, but your version of later has a stage attached and a schedule you do not set, which clarifies wonderfully. People who catch on develop a professional hygiene that others admire without understanding. Nothing fudged, no claims that need managing, hard conversations had in offices before they can happen in hallways: not sainthood, just a clear grasp of which options were ever available. A subtler layer sits under the visible one. Ambition itself can be a burial site, a summit chased partly to avoid the question of what you would want if you stopped climbing, and that question also returns, often as a flatness arriving at the exact moment of an achievement. It deserves the same early handling as any misstatement: faced quietly, before it stages a scene of its own. The public half of the bargain turns out better than it first appears. A working life run on the assumption that everything eventually shows becomes, in the long run, one of the sturdiest standings in any field, not because you never erred but because nothing about you requires maintenance. What shows in view matches what stands behind it, and you learned the match early, for the excellent reason that you had to.

Envy, in your chart, is a carrier pigeon. The eleventh house holds friends, circles, and the hopes you keep for the long run, and the Lot of Nemesis sits there, which means the things you decline to face tend to be social ones, and the news about them arrives through other people's lives. The sting when a friend lands something you never even tried for is not pettiness; it is a buried hope reporting its location. The flash of relief when a group plan collapses is information about how you actually feel in that group. What gets put away in this house wears familiar faces: the friendship that went quiet and was allowed to stay quiet, the role in the circle you resent and keep performing, the hope you renounced out loud and kept anyway, which stirs every time someone near you reaches it. Left alone, these things resolve the eleventh-house way, through the slow social fade, the falling-out that was five years in the making, the group that dissolves over a grievance nobody ever spoke. Attended to, they are unusually easy to reach, because the messengers keep arriving. Each envy names a want. Each dodge names a doubt. Reading them takes honesty rather than courage, since nobody else ever has to know what the pigeon said. The circle steadies as you do it, and the hopes you actually hold, once admitted, turn out to have been waiting with remarkable patience for you to come back for them.

The twelfth house is the part of a life that happens with the door shut: solitude, sleep, the inner rooms, the big institutions whose corridors the public never walks. Your Lot of Nemesis keeps to those rooms. Saturn's own among the computed lots, it collects whatever a person prefers not to look at, so the arrangement doubles here: the hidden point in the hidden house. What you put away can be hidden even from you. You may not experience yourself as avoiding anything, and that is precisely the signature. The material goes down whole, without a splash, and reports back indirectly: a mood that arrives with no visible cause, a dream that repeats until you finally write it down, a pattern you only see in retrospect, three similar endings in a row, the same strange undoing of good situations. None of this is enemy action. It deserves saying plainly, because twelfth-house language has frightened people for centuries: nothing in you is plotting your downfall. Buried things push toward the surface because they are trying to get handled, the way a splinter works its way out, and the discomfort of the pushing is the healing, not the wound. Your reckonings prefer privacy, which is a mercy with a condition attached. The condition is that you actually provide the privacy. Things in you come up when it is quiet, on the long walk, in the empty house, in the second week of any real rest, and if quiet never happens they wait, and press, and lean on the machinery. This is why stillness can feel oddly threatening to you: it is never empty, and some part of you knows what is scheduled to speak there. The temptation is to stay busy forever, and the whole art here is declining that temptation on purpose. Regular, unheroic quiet, taken before it is forced, turns the process gentle. A thing allowed to come up on a Tuesday evening is a thought, sometimes a sad one, occasionally a big one, but a thought, met by a person with attention to give it. The same thing denied its Tuesday for a decade meets you differently. People built like you do much of their important work in this hidden theater, feeling things through alone, forgiving in private, letting go of what nobody knew they held. An old edge gone, a lightness with no visible source: changes like that come out of this room. The walk at dusk when something you did not know you were carrying finally says its name is usually smaller than the silence made it. Almost everything is.
